items.title: Randy Brecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 12, 2022
items.q: Bassist — I don’t know if you know bassist Frank Tate but this goes back 21 years.

ctx.x: Well I did and occasionally I do. It’s hard to tell what it is unless they mark it. But the residuals have been less and less. You know back in the day you could almost live off, honestly, the residuals that you could make particularly from the jingles. I had done more jingle work than Mike because — and this was a conscious decision on his part — he didn’t want to be [inaudible] speak. He wanted to concentrate on the tenor saxophone. He even didn’t want to play, after a while, soprano. He had one and he played…

I see. I’m glad you brought up Ada’s name, your wife, and I flashed to this little thing I’m going to run by you. Bassist — I don’t know if you know bassist Frank Tate but this goes back 21 years. But I asked him, the question I had for him was what’s it like to make a living as a professional musician. And his answer was, “Well I have a wife who has a real job so it’s not too bad.” So is it challenging for both of you to be in the music business or have you sort of worked out the mechanism?

Well you know like I said, I was lucky to come to New York when I did, wanting to be a freelance player because then there was a lot of work, studio work for those who lent themselves to that. You had to have a certain kind of personality and a certain kind of well rounded way of playing and like different styles of music. I just fit into that mindset pretty easily as did my brother and a lot of the studio musicians. But Broadway was happening — there’s problems there now with electronic orchestras taking over,…
